SK2044 The equality members are inconsistent with each other

A type declares one half of an equality or ordering contract and not the other: Equals(Self) with no IEquatable<Self>, or == and IComparable with no relational operators.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since1.3
SupersedesS1210, S3897

Why

Each is one decision written down once and not the second time, and each leaves two spellings of the same question giving different answers. A typed Equals(Self) that no interface advertises is invisible to EqualityComparer<T>.Default, to Dictionary<Self, …> and to every where T : IEquatable<T> constraint, so the type is compared through the object overload it was written to avoid — boxing on a struct, and identity on a class that has no override. A type that defines == and also orders itself, without < and >, offers half an operator set and sends the reader to CompareTo to find out whether the other half exists.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Key {
    public int Id { get; init; }

    public bool Equals(Key? other) => other is not null && other.Id == Id;

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Key key && Equals(key);

    public override int GetHashCode() => Id;
}

Write:

sealed class Key : IEquatable<Key> {
    public int Id { get; init; }

    public bool Equals(Key? other) => other is not null && other.Id == Id;

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Key key && Equals(key);

    public override int GetHashCode() => Id;
}

When it does not fire

⚠ One finding per type, in a fixed order, never one per sub-case. The two are aspects of a single omission, and reporting them separately would multiply one decision by how many ways it shows. ⚠ `SK2004`'s span is left to `SK2004`: a type implementing IEquatable<Self> with no Equals(object) override is that rule's finding, and this one asks its precondition first and stays silent where it holds — by construction, not by a severity filter, so neither rule can be turned on into a duplicate. The typed Equals must take exactly the declaring type and return bool, so Equals(string) on something that is not a string is an overload rather than a contract; an explicit interface implementation counts as implementing the interface. Records are excluded, because the compiler writes all of it. The ordering half fires only on a type that already declares ==, which is what separates a type in the operator business from the many that implement IComparable<T> so a Sort call works and want no operators at all; CA1036 covers the same ground and was measured not to fire at the SDK's recommended analysis level, which is why this half stands. ⚠ `S3875`'s core — `operator ==` with no `Equals(object)` override — was built and then withdrawn. A probe compiled against a real project reports it as CS0660 and CS0661: compiler warnings, always on, needing no analyzer package and no configuration. Restating a diagnostic the compiler already emits is the double-count doc 17 excludes on sight, and it would have shipped had the probe not been compiled. ⚠ `S4035` — "classes implementing `IEquatable<T>` should be sealed" — is declined rather than implemented. Unsealed is not the defect; the defect is an Equals that accepts a derived instance through an is T test, so that a base and a derived instance compare equal in one direction and not the other. That is a different analysis with a different false-positive story, it needs its own id and its own measurement, and a shape-only finding on every unsealed IEquatable<T> would report the many that handle it correctly. Fixless — adding IEquatable<Self> to a base list changes a public surface, and an operator set cannot be generated from an ordering. Each is a review, not a text edit. ⚠ A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading. On the reference trees a class declaring IEquatable<Self> was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an error type, so the interface list held IEquatable<> and the comparison against System.IEquatable1 failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.
